we-the-people-1787-1791.works: The 1790 pies read at a glance: Virginia's big pie and the large orange shares in Virginia and the Carolinas jump out, and one pop-up gives total, percentage, House seats, senators and the counted-in-full / not-counted seat numbers in plain sentences, so Q1 and Q3 need almost no explaining from me. On the ratification layer the close votes show as near-even half-and-half pies.

findings.where: Picture q2-seats (House seats in 1793 turned on); Ratifying the Constitution pies and labels drawing on top; Seats in Congress, step 2 (read the labels) and the most/fewest answer
findings.what: I turn on House seats and get two sets of labels: 'VA: 19', 'PA: 13', 'NY: 10', 'NC: 10', and also 'VA 10', 'PA 2', 'NY 11', 'NC 12', 'RI 13', 'NC (1788)', plus dark blue-and-orange pies that aren't the population pies. The sheet says each label is a state and its seats, so a kid will tell me Rhode Island had 13 seats and Pennsylvania 2.
findings.why: Q2 is answered from the labels. If ratification order numbers look like seat counts, a good part of the class writes wrong answers and I only find out when grading. I've never used ArcGIS, so I wouldn't think to look for a layer the list says is off.
findings.suggestion: Make sure Ratifying the Constitution is really off in the saved map until Q4. The layer list says it is off, but its pies and labels are drawing in this picture; I'd check the saved visibility. Also give the ratification labels a form that can't be read as seats, e.g. 'RI ratified 13th'.
findings.evidence: we-the-people-1787-1791--q2-seats.png (labels NY 11, RI 13, VA 10, NC 12, PA 2 next to NY: 10, VA: 19, PA: 13, NC: 10)

findings.where: Picture q2-seats; House seats in 1793 labels; Seats in Congress, step 2 and 'which the fewest'
findings.what: The seat labels I can read are VA: 19, PA: 13, NY: 10, NC: 10, CT: 7, KY: 2 and GA: 2. There's no DE: 1, and no NJ, MD or SC label. The small mid-Atlantic states are buried under pies, and the population pies show faintly through the blue shading. From the labels, 'fewest' looks like a tie at 2.
findings.why: The answer notes want Delaware (1). Students reading labels will miss it, and I'd end up telling them to click Delaware, which defeats the point of the labels.
findings.suggestion: In Q2, have students turn off Population in 1790 and open the New England and New York bookmark (or zoom in on the mid-Atlantic) before reading labels; or set the seat labels to always show, with no label collision.
findings.evidence: we-the-people-1787-1791--q2-seats.png

findings.where: Picture q4-ratify (only Ratifying the Constitution on); its labels; How close was ratification?, steps 3-4 (click the pies; find North Carolina's two pies)
findings.what: Each label sits up and to the right of its pie, so it lands beside the next pie up the coast. 'NC (1788)' sits on the pie in Virginia, 'VA 10' sits by Maryland's pie, 'NC 12' sits beside the mostly orange Hillsborough pie, and 'RI 13' sits on the big Massachusetts pie. MA 6, CT 5, NJ 3 and DE 1 don't show at all.
findings.why: Step 4 says find North Carolina's two pies. Students will click the pie under 'NC (1788)' and get Virginia. Massachusetts is one of the three closest votes and has no label. Pop-up titles rescue them, but it eats minutes and trips me up at the front too.
findings.suggestion: Center each label on its pie, or put it directly below, or turn off label collision for this layer. Add 'Open the New England and New York bookmark' to Q4 so the crowded northern pies separate.
findings.evidence: we-the-people-1787-1791--q4-ratify.png; we-the-people-1787-1791--q4-nc.png (the Fayetteville pie, the 12th state, sits just below the 'SC 8' label)

findings.where: Picture q1-virginia, pop-up first line (Who lived where in 1790?, step 3); picture q4-nc, pop-up first line (How close was ratification?, step 3); legend headings in open and q2-seats
findings.what: The percentage reads '(39.099998474121094%)'. The North Carolina vote reads 'Ratified on 11/21/1789, 12:00 AM'. The legend headings are 'Total1790' and 'HouseSeats'.
findings.why: Kids will copy all seventeen digits, and a midnight timestamp looks like a glitch. On the projector it makes the map look unfinished.
findings.suggestion: Round the percentage to one decimal (39.1%), show the date as November 21, 1789 with no time, and rename the legend headings (e.g. 'People in 1790', 'House seats in 1793').
findings.evidence: Pop-up text: '1790 census: 747,610 people, 292,627 of them enslaved (39.099998474121094%).' and 'Ratified on 11/21/1789, 12:00 AM: 194 for, 77 against.'; legend text 'Total1790', 'HouseSeats'

findings.where: Picture open (Population in 1790); the Massachusetts pie; Who lived where in 1790?, steps 2-3
findings.what: The second-biggest pie in the north sits in the middle of Maine, and Massachusetts itself has no pie. Clicking it says 'Massachusetts in 1790'.
findings.why: The sheet warns that Maine is shown within Massachusetts, so most students will cope, but some will write 'Maine' or tell me Massachusetts is missing.
findings.suggestion: Place the Massachusetts pie inside Massachusetts proper, using a hand-placed point instead of the center of Massachusetts plus Maine.
findings.evidence: we-the-people-1787-1791--open.png; q2-seats pop-up 'Includes Maine (96,540 people), then part of Massachusetts.'

rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-liv.works: The district pop-up is one plain sentence with name, party, state and district number, and the topographic basemap makes our own town and streets easy to recognize. The historic-places pop-up gives the place's name as its title, which is better than the sheet promises.

findings.where: App tools (Basemaps, Map layers, Legend, Measure, Sketch, 2D/3D, Bookmarks; no search); open view of the whole country; Who represents us?, step 1, and every later 'zoom in on your town' step
findings.what: The map opens on the whole continent, there's only one bookmark (The United States) and no search box. My kids have to pan and zoom by eye to find our town.
findings.why: Thirty 8th graders hunting for their town on Chromebooks eats several minutes of a 15-minute question, and some will end up in the next town over.
findings.suggestion: Add the app's search tool so students can type the town or school name.
findings.evidence: Tool list and bookmark list in the packet; rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live--open.png

findings.where: Picture open (zoomed out); Congressional districts (119th Congress); Who represents us?, step 4 and 'How many districts does your state have?'
findings.what: Every line is the same blue. State borders look exactly like district lines, and no district is numbered. In my state I'd be counting blobs, and around the cities they're too small to count.
findings.why: Students will come up with different counts and I'll spend time refereeing. In a big state the count is basically impossible.
findings.suggestion: Put the state's total in the pop-up ('Ohio Congressional District 15 of 15'), or draw state borders heavier than district lines and label each district with its number.
findings.evidence: rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live--open.png

findings.where: Pictures q1-district and q4-nrhp (Columbus, zoomed in to street level); Topographic basemap; Rights in public places, steps 1-2, and Responsibilities, step 1
findings.what: Even at street level I see street names, neighborhoods, parks, a stadium and a shopping center, but no courthouse, city hall or library. Capitol Square is an unlabeled green block with no 'Ohio Statehouse'.
findings.why: Q2 and Q3 depend on students finding four labeled public buildings. If those labels only appear at the very last zoom level, or not at all in our town, the class stalls and I need a fallback.
findings.suggestion: Check how far in you have to zoom before building labels appear in a few towns, and put that in the sheet ('zoom in until you can see individual buildings'). Better still, add a points layer of public buildings (libraries, post offices, courthouses) that students can click.
findings.evidence: rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live--q1-district.png; rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live--q4-nrhp.png

findings.where: Picture q4-nrhp-click; National Register of Historic Places pop-up; Reading the map and History where we live, step 3
findings.what: The sheet says the pop-up gives an address but not a name, and sends students to the basemap label or the National Archives link. The pop-up I got is titled 'Ohio Statehouse'.
findings.why: Students waste time on a link and a basemap label they don't need, and I look unprepared when they say 'it does have a name'.
findings.suggestion: Change the sheet to: 'The pop-up's title gives the place's name, and its Resource Type line says whether it's a building, district or site.' Make the same fix in About this map and the answer notes.
findings.evidence: Pop-up text: 'Ohio Statehouse / Property ID: 72001011 / SE corner of High and Broad Sts. ... Resource Type: building'

findings.where: Pictures q4-nrhp and q4-nrhp-click; National Register diamonds; History where we live, steps 2-3 ('the two nearest your school', 'the basemap label under the diamond')
findings.what: The diamond that opened 'Ohio Statehouse, SE corner of High and Broad' sits on High Street at the freeway by the Brewery District, several blocks south of the green Capitol Square. The pop-up also says 1 of 2.
findings.why: If diamonds aren't on their buildings, 'the two nearest the school' and 'the label under the diamond' send kids to the wrong place.
findings.suggestion: I'd check a few points in this layer against their addresses. If many are off, drop 'read the name from the basemap label' from the sheet and rely on the pop-up title and address.
findings.evidence: rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live--q4-nrhp-click.png (highlighted diamond by the freeway, 1 of 2); rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live--q4-nrhp.png (Capitol Square by the 'Columbus' label)

findings.where: Picture q4-nrhp, National Register legend; History where we live, step 4 ('use the legend to tell a building from a district or a site')
findings.what: Building is dark teal and site is dark maroon, and on diamonds this small they look alike. Structure and object are pale yellow and pale sage that fade into the basemap. In the Columbus view every diamond looks the same teal.
findings.why: Students can't reliably do step 4 by color. The pop-up's Resource Type line is the dependable way.
findings.suggestion: Point step 4 at the pop-up's Resource Type line, and give building, district and site clearly different colors or shapes.
findings.evidence: rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live--q4-nrhp.png (legend and diamonds)

presidential-elections-1796-1800.works: The orange and blue pies are clear, and the thin Adams slivers in Pennsylvania, Virginia and North Carolina are visible at laptop size. The pop-up title gives the state and its electors, and the votes line gives exactly what Q1-Q3 ask for. Zoomed in, the two court cases sit far enough apart to measure easily.

findings.where: Picture q4-marbury (zoomed in on Washington and Baltimore); Landmark Supreme Court cases, the Marbury v. Madison square; The Supreme Court, near the capital, steps 1-2
findings.what: I click the Marbury v. Madison square and nothing opens. McCulloch's pop-up works.
findings.why: Half of Q4 ('what happened in each place') comes from the Why here part. With no pop-up the class can't answer it from the map, and I'd be supplying it from memory.
findings.suggestion: Check that the Marbury feature has its pop-up turned on with the same template as McCulloch, and that nothing else (a label or the Maryland pie) is catching the click.
findings.evidence: presidential-elections-1796-1800--q4-marbury.png: '(no pop-up opened)'

findings.where: Pictures open and q4-mcculloch (opening view); Landmark Supreme Court cases on top of Maryland's Election of 1796 pie (and 1800); The election of 1796, step 3; The election of 1800, steps 2-3; Supreme Court, step 1
findings.what: At the opening zoom the two pink squares overlap each other and sit on top of Maryland's pie. The only label, 'Marbury v. Madison (1803)', sits over the upper square, which is actually McCulloch. Maryland is a split state in both elections, and most of its pie is hidden.
findings.why: Students who click Maryland get a court case instead of the vote split, and students who click 'Marbury' by its label get McCulloch. The sheet's Q4 never says to zoom in (the front steps do).
findings.suggestion: Have the cases layer off when the map opens and turned on in Q4, or make it show only when zoomed in. Make step 1 of the sheet's Q4 'Zoom in on Maryland until the two pink squares separate'.
findings.evidence: presidential-elections-1796-1800--open.png; presidential-elections-1796-1800--q4-mcculloch.png (highlighted McCulloch square is the upper one, under the Marbury label)

findings.where: Picture q2-1800 (1796 off, 1800 on); pop-up; The election of 1800, step 1, and Which states switched?, step 1
findings.what: After I switch to 1800, Pennsylvania's 1796 pop-up is still open and the state is still highlighted. Its title, 'Pennsylvania: 15 electors', doesn't say which year.
findings.why: Students who switch layers with a pop-up open will copy 1796 numbers into the 1800 answer. That's the kind of mix-up I only discover while grading.
findings.suggestion: Put the year in the pop-up title ('Pennsylvania in 1796: 15 electors'), and add 'Close any open pop-up' to the layer-switching steps.
findings.evidence: presidential-elections-1796-1800--q2-1800.png (pop-up reads 'Electors' votes in 1796' over the 1800 layer)

louisiana-purchase-1803-1806.works: Q1 works cleanly: the yellow purchase next to the green 1783 land shows 'about double' at a glance, and the pop-up gives the exact fill-in numbers (530,000,000 acres, $15 million). The Across the Rockies bookmark shows the trail leaving the yellow at the mountains and an unshaded Pacific coast, so Q4's first two answers are right there.

findings.where: Pictures q3-biomes (Up the Missouri bookmark, Biomes on) and q3-biome-click (zoomed out); Biomes layer; Up the Missouri, steps 3-4
findings.what: At the Up the Missouri bookmark with Biomes on, I see no biome colors at all: just the same yellow as the purchase, the gray-green 1783 land and the purple Texas strip, with brown watershed outlines still drawn. Clicking the shading along the route opened 'Souris-Red-Rainy Region, HUC ID: 09' (1 of 3), which is a watershed. The grassland pop-up only came up in the zoomed-out view.
findings.why: A student following the steps writes a watershed name as the biome, or gets nothing. I don't know ArcGIS well enough to guess that a layer only draws at some zoom levels, so the class would stall.
findings.suggestion: Set the Biomes layer's visible range to include the Up the Missouri bookmark's scale (or change the bookmark), and check that turning off United States Watersheds really hides its HUC sub-layers in the app. Until then, add 'zoom out two steps' to step 4.
findings.evidence: louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--q3-biomes.png (shading matches the purchase yellow in louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--open.png; pop-up 'Souris-Red-Rainy Region HUC ID: 09'); louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--q3-biome-click.png

findings.where: Pictures open and q1-purchase; Lewis and Clark campsites (approximate) and National Historic Trail; Across the Rockies, steps 3-4 (find the eastern end at Pittsburgh, measure to the Pacific)
findings.what: The orange campsite dots are so dense they hide the purple line the sheet describes; the purple only shows where camps are sparse. East of where the line ends at Pittsburgh there are several more scattered dots out toward the Chesapeake.
findings.why: Students told to start at 'the trail's eastern end' will click the farthest dot east. That adds a few hundred miles and pushes them out of the 2,100-2,300 range the answer notes accept.
findings.suggestion: Make the campsite dots smaller (or show them only when zoomed in) so the purple line reads. Either drop the dots east of Pittsburgh or have the sheet say 'start where the purple line ends at Pittsburgh, not at the separate dots further east'.
findings.evidence: louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--open.png; louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--q1-purchase.png (dots east of the line's end)

findings.where: Pictures open and q2-watersheds (legend open); the green 1783 land and the Ohio Region outline; A bigger country, step 2, and Why New Orleans?, step 2
findings.what: With the legend open, it covers most of the green 1783 land and the whole Ohio River basin. All I see of the green is a strip at the right edge.
findings.why: Q1 compares yellow with green and Q2 starts at the Ohio outline. Students who leave the legend open will compare against a sliver and won't find the Ohio region.
findings.suggestion: Add 'Close the legend' to step 2 of Q1 and Q2 (the app's panel may sit differently, but I'd check it at Chromebook size).
findings.evidence: louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--open.png; louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--q2-watersheds.png

findings.where: Picture q1-purchase (pop-up) and picture q3-biome-click (pop-up); A bigger country answer notes; Up the Missouri, step 4
findings.what: The answer notes say the purchase pop-up has Notes and an 'Area in Square Kilometers' field to back up 'about double'. The pop-up I got is one sentence with neither. The biome pop-up adds a 'Nature Could Recover ... Half Protected' paragraph about conservation status.
findings.why: I'd go looking for the km² figure to settle arguments and it isn't there. The conservation paragraph is jargon my 8th graders will ask about mid-lesson.
findings.suggestion: Either add the area to the purchase and 1783 pop-ups or drop it from the answer notes. Remove the conservation-status lines from the Biomes pop-up.
findings.evidence: Pop-up text: 'The Louisiana Purchase encompassed 530,000,000 acres ... for $15 million.' and 'Nature Could Recover / The amount of protected and unprotected natural habitat remaining is less than 50% ...'

war-of-1812-and-monroe-doctrine.works: At the War of 1812 bookmark the three clusters (Great Lakes, Chesapeake, Gulf Coast) and the biggest diamonds are obvious, and the New Orleans pop-up puts date, victor and casualties at the top. Blue circles and orange diamonds differ in shape as well as color, and the recognition and treaty-line pop-ups give exactly the date or description each question needs.

findings.where: Picture q3-boundary (The 1819 boundary bookmark, both layers on); Land Spain gave up in 1819 and Adams-Onís Treaty line, 1819; Florida and a new border, steps 1, 3 and 4
findings.what: The bookmark is centered on the West. Florida is only a sliver at the far right edge beside the legend, and the Gulf end of the dashed line (the Sabine River, part 1) runs under the legend. The only green inside the frame is a small patch in the Rockies.
findings.why: Step 3 says to click the green land, so students will click the Rockies patch instead of Florida, and they can't start the line at part 1. The Florida and part 1 pop-ups in these pictures were only reached by zooming way out.
findings.suggestion: Reframe the bookmark to run from Florida to the Pacific (one zoom level further out), or add a second bookmark for Florida. Tell students to close the legend before clicking.
findings.evidence: war-of-1812-and-monroe-doctrine--q3-boundary.png; war-of-1812-and-monroe-doctrine--q3-florida.png and war-of-1812-and-monroe-doctrine--q3-treatyline.png (both taken zoomed out)

findings.where: Picture q3-florida; East Florida pop-up on Land Spain gave up in 1819; Florida and a new border, step 3 and its answer
findings.what: The pop-up says the United States agreed to 'assume $5 million in damage caused by American citizens when they rebelled against Spain'.
findings.why: As I remember it, the US took on up to $5 million of American citizens' claims against Spain, not damage Americans caused. Students will copy this sentence into their answer, and I'd be teaching against my own map.
findings.suggestion: I'd check Article 11 of the treaty (the Avalon Project text the treaty-line pop-ups already link to) and rewrite the note, e.g. 'The United States agreed to pay up to $5 million in claims that American citizens had against Spain.'
findings.evidence: Pop-up text: 'While the Americans didn't pay Spain for the land, they did agree to assume $5 million in damage caused by American citizens when they rebelled against Spain'

findings.where: Picture q4-latin (Latin America in 1825 bookmark, recognition layer on); labels on Latin American independence and US recognition, plus the 1800 country labels; New nations and the Monroe Doctrine, steps 3-4
findings.what: Labels sit up and to the right of their symbols. 'Paraguay 1811' lands right on Brazil's blue circle, Brazil has no label, and Paraguay's orange diamond sits under a big italic 'Peru' from the 1800 map. The sheet says the map has no place names, but it's full of them (United States, Louisiana, New Spain of Mexico, Cuba, Peru).
findings.why: A student skimming labels will list Paraguay as recognized by 1824 and wonder why there are two Perus. Clicking fixes it, but some won't click.
findings.suggestion: Place these labels directly below or centered on each symbol (or turn off collision so 'Brazil 1822' shows), and hide the 1800 country labels at this bookmark. Fix 'no place names' in the sheet.
findings.evidence: war-of-1812-and-monroe-doctrine--q4-latin.png

findings.where: Picture q2-neworleans (pop-up); Battles of the War of 1812; Where was the war fought?, step 2 (front steps: 'read the battle name and State Name')
findings.what: The pop-up gives the battle name, date, 'American Side Victory' and casualties, but no state or place. It also doesn't show the field names (State Name, Battle Dates, Battle Victor) that the front steps tell me to read out.
findings.why: New Orleans is easy, but for battles named after forts or creeks students can't say where they were. When I read the front steps I won't find what they promise. Students can still name the three regions from the clusters, so it's not fatal.
findings.suggestion: Add a line such as 'Fought in: Louisiana' to the battle pop-up, or reword the front steps and answer notes to match what the pop-up shows.
findings.evidence: Pop-up text: 'New Orleans / January 8, 1815 / American Side Victory / Total Casualties: 2,096 ...'

findings.where: Pictures q4-circle and q2-neworleans (pop-ups) and the battle legend in q1-bookmark; New nations, step 3; The biggest battles, step 2
findings.what: The recognition date reads '1/27/1823, 12:00 AM'. The New Orleans pop-up repeats its last paragraph word for word. The casualties legend starts at '< 0'.
findings.why: Small things, but students ask about the midnight time and the 'less than zero' casualties, and the repeated paragraph looks careless on the projector.
findings.suggestion: Show dates as January 27, 1823 with no time, remove the duplicate paragraph, and start the size legend at the smallest real casualty count.
findings.evidence: Pop-up text: 'Recognized by the United States: 1/27/1823, 12:00 AM.'; New Orleans pop-up's final paragraph appears twice; legend text '< 0'
